newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON WASHOUT LEAVES ORGANISERS WITH BIG BACKLOG.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WIMBLEDON WASHOUT LEAVES ORGANISERS WITH BIG BACKLOG.

text.p: Play was abandoned without a ball being hit on the fourth day of the Wimbledon championships after constant rain made Thursday a washout.
It was the first time since 1992 than an entire day had been lost to rain and left organisers with a huge backlog of matches.
"We are approximately 120 or 130 matches behind," said tournament referee Alan Mills, who must now consider whether play should take place on Sunday.
The middle Sunday of the Grand Slam event is a rest day but in 1991, when the rain was even worse, it was used as a catch-up day for the first time in the tournament's history.
The day was a huge success among tennis fans who queued for cheap tickets and turned Centre Court, normally the site of typically English restraint and decorum, into a carnival.
"I personally thought the middle Sunday in 1991 was probably the most inspiring day that I have ever spent at Wimbledon," said Mills. "The atmosphere was electric."

Given fine weather, the entire first and second rounds of the singles -- 192 matches in all -- should have been completed by Thursday evening plus a good chunk of the three doubles events. But so far this week only 96 matches have finished.
"We have 26 ladies who have not played their first round singles and we have got six men who are unfinished in their first round singles," Mills said.
At the same stage in 1991, only 52 matches had been completed in nine hours 15 minutes of play.
Organisers have brought forward the start of play on Friday and Saturday but Mills said the weather prospects were poor.
"The weather forecast is very depressing but obviously we have got to press on and take each day as it comes and try to do what we can," he said.
"It is the wettest day that I can remember. We are waiting to hear just how much rain has fallen -- it is certainly a lot."
Mills said no decision on whether to play on Sunday could be made before organisers had consulted the police, local authority and caterers and other suppliers.

Security has been stepped up at this year's championships, following the Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb scare at the Grand National in April and Mills said organisers would have to make sure they could provide adequate security if the grounds were opened on Sunday.
But the weather might have the last word. Mills said the forecast for Sunday was gloomy.
"As far as we can see into it, it is five days of not too hopeful weather. There isn't one day you can say it is going to be a fine, sunny day, even in the middle of flaming June."
If the weather rules out trying to play on Sunday, Mills said the tournament could be extended into a third week.
"We can go on until we finish. I think the third Tuesday would be our deadline. Player have other commitments and other tournaments," he said.

Other emergency measures could include reducing the men's singles to the best of three sets, at least for some of the rounds, he said. The men's doubles have already been cut from best of five up to the quarter-final stage.
On a rain-free day, Wimbledon's 18 courts could see about 110 three-set matches, Mills said.
Organisers defended their decision not to put a retractable roof on the new Court One which was officially opened on Monday.
"It is just not practical," said order of play committee chairman Tim Phillips. "This is an outdoor tournament, a grasscourt tournament."
